specStatements.text: When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other they become electrically charged. Negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons is left with an equal positive charge.

When two electrically charged objects are brought close together they exert a force on each other. Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel. Two objects that carry different types of charge attract. Attraction and repulsion between two charged objects are examples of non-contact force.
• describe the production of static electricity, and sparking, by rubbing surfaces
• describe evidence that charged objects exert forces of attraction or repulsion on one another when not in contact
• explain how the transfer of electrons between objects can explain the phenomena of static electricity.
A charged object creates an electric field around itself. The electric field is strongest close to the charged object. The further away from the charged object, the weaker the field.
A second charged object placed in the field experiences a force. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
• draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
• explain the concept of an electric field
• explain how the concept of an electric field helps to explain the non-contact force between charged objects as well as other electrostatic phenomena such as sparking.

scopeNotes.statement: • draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the isolated charged sphere is drawn or asked about: straight radial lines spreading out in every direction, evenly spaced around the sphere, drawn closer together near the surface where the field is strongest, with arrows pointing away from a positive sphere and towards a negative one. No field pattern for a pair of charges, for parallel plates, or for any combination of overlapping fields is taught or tested, because the specification names only the isolated sphere. Because drawing cannot be marked by a multiple-choice item, the drawing skill is assessed by asking students to identify the correct description of the pattern (q15) and to explain the line spacing (c15, m09, m10, m16).

scopeNotes.statement: When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other they become electrically charged.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Charging by rubbing is applied only to insulating materials, exactly as the specification words it, and never presented as something every material will do. Where a metal appears (q04) it is used only to show that charge placed on a conductor held in the hand flows away to earth; no quantitative treatment of conduction, earthing, charging by induction, or the triboelectric series is introduced, since none of that is in this section.

scopeNotes.statement: A second charged object placed in the field experiences a force. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The link between force and distance is kept purely qualitative, in the specification's own words: closer means stronger. No inverse-square law, no formula for the force between two charges, no field-strength equation and no numerical field or force calculation is used anywhere in this section, because the specification states only the direction of the change.

concepts.definition: Electric charge that has built up on an object and stays where it is instead of flowing as a current. It is produced when certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other.
When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other, leaving both materials charged.
The movement of negatively charged electrons from one material to another. No charge is created or destroyed; it is only moved.
An object that has gained electrons, so it has more electrons than the positive charge in it can balance.
An object that has lost electrons, so the positive charge left in it is no longer balanced.
The charges produced by rubbing are always equal in size and opposite in sign, because every electron lost by one material is gained by the other.
A material through which charge cannot flow easily, so charge placed on it stays where it is put. Charging by rubbing works with certain insulating materials.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge push each other apart.
Two objects that carry different types of charge pull each other together.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between charged objects are examples of a non-contact force.
A sudden flow of charge across a gap, seen and heard as a spark, which happens when enough charge has built up on a surface.
When the electric field in a gap becomes strong enough, the air in the gap stops behaving as an insulator and allows charge to flow across, producing a spark.
The region around a charged object in which a second charged object experiences a force.
The electric field is strongest close to the charged object and gets weaker the further away from it you go.

concepts.term: Field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
concepts.definition: Straight field lines spreading out radially in all directions from the sphere, evenly spaced around it and closer together near the surface, with arrows pointing away from a positive sphere and towards a negative one.

concepts.term: Force on a second charged object
concepts.definition: A charged object placed in an electric field experiences a force, and that force gets stronger as the distance between the two objects decreases.

concepts.term: Field explanation of a non-contact force
concepts.definition: Each charged object sits inside the electric field of the other, so each one experiences a force without the two ever touching.
A charged rod hung on a thread so that it can turn freely, used as evidence that a second charged rod brought near it, but not touching, can push it away or pull it round.

misconceptions.question: Does rubbing two materials together make new electric charge?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rubbing only transfers electrons that were already there from one material to the other. No charge is made or destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing creates charge, in the same way that rubbing your hands creates heat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and the phrase 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during the rubbing, so the transfer is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges always appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, and that never happens.

misconceptions.question: Which particles move when two insulating materials are rubbed together?
misconceptions.correct: Electrons move. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the material that loses them is left positively charged.
misconceptions.misconception: Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other, because a positive charge appears.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A student who sees a positive charge appear assumes that positive particles must have travelled to make it. Protons and electrons are often taught as an equal-and-opposite pair, so they seem equally free to move.
misconceptions.correction: Protons are locked inside the nuclei of the atoms and cannot be rubbed off a surface. Only the outer electrons are loosely enough held to move. A positive charge is what is left behind when electrons leave, not something that arrives.

misconceptions.question: Are the two charges produced by rubbing always the same size?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The charge lost by one material is exactly the charge gained by the other, so the two are equal in size and opposite in sign.
misconceptions.misconception: One material ends up more strongly charged than the other, depending on how hard it was rubbed or what it is made of.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rubbing feels one-sided, because the student holds one object and moves the other, so it seems as though something is done to one object and not the other.
misconceptions.correction: Every electron that leaves one surface arrives on the other, so the counts must match. Rubbing harder transfers more electrons, but it increases both charges together and by the same amount.

misconceptions.question: Can a metal rod held in your bare hand be charged up by rubbing it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Any charge produced flows away through your hand and body, so no charge stays on the rod.
misconceptions.misconception: Any object can be given a static charge by rubbing it hard enough; metal simply needs more rubbing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charging by rubbing is demonstrated with rods that look ordinary, so students treat it as a property of rubbing rather than of the material. The word 'insulating' in the specification is easy to skip over.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says certain insulating materials. Charge stays put on an insulator, but a metal conducts, so charge produced on a hand-held metal rod immediately leaks away through the person to earth. Held on an insulating handle, the same metal rod does keep its charge.

misconceptions.question: What happens when two objects carrying the same type of charge are brought close?
misconceptions.correct: They repel: they push each other apart. Only objects carrying different types of charge attract.
misconceptions.misconception: Charged objects always attract other charged objects, so two objects with the same charge still pull together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first demonstrations of static electricity are attractions - a charged rod picking up paper or bending a stream of water - so students generalise that charge means attraction.
misconceptions.correction: Test it with two rods charged in the same way, which must carry the same type of charge: hung on a thread, they swing apart. Like repels like, unlike attracts.

misconceptions.question: Do two charged objects have to touch before they can push or pull each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. The force acts across a gap, which is why it is called a non-contact force.
misconceptions.misconception: A push or a pull needs contact, so the objects only affect each other at the moment they touch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday forces are contact forces - pushing, pulling, hitting - so a force acting across empty space feels like it needs an explanation the student does not yet have.
misconceptions.correction: The suspended rod starts turning before the second rod reaches it, and it keeps turning while a visible gap remains. The force is already acting across that gap.

misconceptions.question: Is the force between two rubbed rods a magnetic force?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is an electrostatic force, caused by the charge that rubbing has transferred.
misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing magnetises the rod, which is why it can push and pull things without touching them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnetism is the student's only earlier example of a non-contact push and pull, so a new non-contact force is filed under the label they already have.
misconceptions.correction: Rubbing moves electrons; it does not magnetise anything. Polythene and acetate are not magnetic materials at all, and a charged rod attracts small pieces of paper, which no magnet will do.

misconceptions.question: What do the lines in an electric field diagram represent?
misconceptions.correct: They show the direction of the force that a positive charge would feel at each point in the field.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines are routes that a charge has to follow, like rails or wires running out from the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The lines are drawn as solid, continuous marks, which look like tracks. Students have also seen circuit diagrams, where lines really are wires that carry charge.
misconceptions.correction: The lines are a way of drawing the field on paper; nothing runs along them. They tell you which way the force points and, by how closely they are packed, how strong the field is.

misconceptions.question: What shape are the field lines around an isolated charged sphere?
misconceptions.correct: Straight lines spreading out radially in all directions, evenly spaced around the sphere.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines are circles drawn round the sphere, going all the way around it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse the electric field pattern with contour lines on a map, or with the loops of a magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet.
misconceptions.correction: The force on a charge near a sphere points straight towards or straight away from the centre, so the lines must be radial. A circle would mean the force pushed a charge round the sphere, which it does not.

misconceptions.question: Which way do the arrows point on the field lines around a charged sphere?
misconceptions.correct: Away from a positive sphere and towards a negative sphere, showing the force on a positive charge.
misconceptions.misconception: The arrows always point inwards towards the charged object, because a field pulls things in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gravitational field diagrams are met first and always point inwards, and the word 'field' is remembered as something that attracts.
misconceptions.correction: The arrow shows which way a positive test charge would be pushed. Next to a positive sphere it would be repelled, so the arrows point outwards; only a negative sphere has arrows pointing in.

misconceptions.question: Is there a field in the gaps between the lines on a field diagram?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The field fills the whole region around the charged object; the lines are only a way of drawing it.
misconceptions.misconception: The field only exists along the lines, so a charge sitting in a gap would feel no force at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The diagram shows a small number of separate lines, so the empty paper between them looks like empty space with nothing in it.
misconceptions.correction: You could draw as many lines as you like; drawing more does not add field. A charge placed anywhere near the sphere feels a force, so the field is everywhere around it.

misconceptions.question: How does an electric field change as you move away from the charged object?
misconceptions.correct: It gets weaker. The field is strongest close to the object and weakens with distance.
misconceptions.misconception: The field builds up as it spreads outwards, so it is stronger further away from the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The lines fan out and cover more paper further away, which students read as the field growing rather than thinning out.
misconceptions.correction: Further out, the same number of lines is spread over a larger area, so the lines are further apart and the field is weaker. That is why a spark jumps across a small gap and not a large one.

misconceptions.question: Does moving two charged objects closer together change the force between them?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
misconceptions.misconception: The force depends only on how much charge each object carries, so moving them closer changes nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charge is the quantity written on the diagram and talked about in class, so it becomes the only variable the student thinks the force can depend on.
misconceptions.correction: The second object sits in the first object's field, and that field is strongest close in. Move the objects closer and the field there is stronger, so the force is stronger too.

misconceptions.question: When can charge cross the gap between a charged object and an earthed one?
misconceptions.correct: Charge can cross a gap of air as a spark, before the two ever touch.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge can only move across at the moment the two surfaces actually touch each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is usually taught as something that flows through a conductor, and air is taught as an insulator, so a gap looks like a complete barrier.
misconceptions.correction: The shock from a door handle happens as your hand approaches it, not after contact, and the spark is visible in the gap. A strong enough field lets charge cross the air.

misconceptions.question: What is the spark itself?
misconceptions.correct: It is charge flowing through the air, which conducts once the field across the gap is strong enough.
misconceptions.misconception: Air can never conduct, so a spark must be something else, such as a flash of light or heat from friction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Air is introduced as a good insulator with no exceptions given, so a current in air seems impossible and the light has to be explained some other way.
misconceptions.correction: Air is an insulator only up to a point. A strong enough field pulls electrons off the air particles so that the air conducts, and the flowing charge makes the flash and the crack you hear.

misconceptions.question: How is the spacing of the field lines around a charged sphere chosen?
misconceptions.correct: Lines are drawn closer together where the field is stronger, which is close to the sphere.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines get closer together the further you move away from the sphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that spacing means something without remembering which way round it goes, and lines that meet in the distance look like a familiar perspective drawing.
misconceptions.correction: Close spacing means a strong field. The field is strongest at the surface, so the lines are packed most tightly there and spread further apart as they go out.

misconceptions.question: When a charged rod touches nothing, where is its charge?
misconceptions.correct: It stays where the rubbing put it, because the rod is an insulator.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge always spreads itself out evenly over both objects until they carry the same amount.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sharing to equalise is the rule students learn for heat and for water levels, so they apply the same rule to charge.
misconceptions.correction: Charge only spreads out where it can flow, which means on a conductor. On an insulating rod it stays on the part that was rubbed, which is why one end can attract paper while the other does not.

misconceptions.question: Does the field stop at the last line drawn on the diagram?
misconceptions.correct: No. The field keeps getting weaker with distance but does not have an edge where it ends.
misconceptions.misconception: The field reaches as far as the longest line on the diagram and then stops completely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A diagram has to stop somewhere, and the student reads the edge of the drawing as the edge of the field.
misconceptions.correction: The lines are cut short only to fit on the page. Further out the field is too weak to matter, but there is no distance at which it switches off.

mcqs.stem: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other one.
options.rationale: This is the specification's own account: negatively charged electrons move from one material on to the other, leaving the giver positive and making the receiver negative.

options.text: Rubbing creates fresh charge on the surface of each material.
options.rationale: Students who first met friction as a way of producing heat treat producing static electricity the same way, as making something new rather than moving something already there.

options.text: Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.
options.rationale: A student who sees a positive charge appear assumes that positive particles must have travelled in order to produce it.

options.text: Electrons are rubbed off both materials into the nearby air.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who accept that electrons move but have no destination in mind for them, so the charge is imagined to escape rather than transfer.

mcqs.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What has happened to the cloth?

options.text: It has gained some protons from the rod, so it is positively charged.
options.rationale: The student gets the sign of the cloth right but explains it with moving protons instead of departing electrons.

options.text: It has lost electrons to the rod, so it is now positively charged.
options.rationale: The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and those electrons came from the cloth. Losing electrons leaves the cloth with an equal positive charge.

options.text: It has lost all of its charge, so it now has no charge at all.
options.rationale: Treats charging as one-sided: something is done to the rod, and the cloth is left neutral rather than oppositely charged.

options.text: It has made new positive charge on its surface while rubbing.
options.rationale: The creation misconception applied to the cloth: charge is imagined as being manufactured by the friction rather than left behind by electrons.

mcqs.stem: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material always equal in size to the negative charge on the other?

options.text: Rubbing always produces equal amounts of the two charges at once.
options.rationale: Restates the observation as a rule about rubbing rather than explaining it through electron transfer, which is what the question asks for.

options.text: Both of the materials are rubbed with exactly the same steady force.
options.rationale: Links the size of the charge to how hard the rubbing was, which would make the two charges differ if either object were rubbed harder.

options.text: Every electron lost by one is an electron gained by the other.
options.rationale: The two charges are the two sides of one transfer, so counting electrons on either side must give the same number.

options.text: Charge always spreads out evenly between the two materials.
options.rationale: Applies the sharing rule used for heat, which would also predict equal charges of the same sign rather than opposite ones.

mcqs.stem: A student rubs a metal rod held in her bare hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?

options.text: Metal cannot gain or lose any electrons when it is rubbed.
options.rationale: Blames the particles rather than the conduction, and would wrongly predict that a metal rod on an insulating handle could not be charged either.

options.text: Rubbing a smooth metal surface is unable to create any charge.
options.rationale: Combines the creation misconception with a guess about smoothness, when the real issue is where the charge goes after it is transferred.

options.text: The rod gains and loses equal numbers of electrons as it is rubbed.
options.rationale: An invented balancing mechanism, attractive because it explains a zero result without needing to think about the hand as a conducting path.

options.text: Charge on the rod flows away through her hand and body.
options.rationale: A metal conducts, so any charge produced does not stay on the rod: it leaks to earth through the student. Charging by rubbing needs an insulating material.

mcqs.stem: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Two objects with the same type of charge attract each other.
options.rationale: Held by students whose only experience of static electricity is attraction, such as a charged rod picking up paper.

options.text: Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel each other.
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: like charges repel, and the force acts without the objects touching.

options.text: The objects only push or pull when their surfaces touch.
options.rationale: Denies the non-contact nature of the force, because every force the student has handled before needed contact.

options.text: Two objects with different charges repel one another.
options.rationale: A straight sign reversal, chosen by students who have learned that a rule exists but not which way round it goes.

mcqs.stem: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same dry cloth. One rod hangs freely on a thread. The second rod is held close to it, without touching. What happens, and why?

options.text: The hanging rod swings away, because rubbing magnetised them.
options.rationale: Gets the observation right but files the force under magnetism, the student's only earlier example of a non-contact push.

options.text: The hanging rod swings towards it, because charges attract.
options.rationale: Applies the always-attracts rule, which the paper-and-rod demonstration seems to support.

options.text: The hanging rod swings away, because both carry a like charge.
options.rationale: Rubbing both rods in the same way gives both the same type of charge, and like charges repel across the gap between them.

options.text: The hanging rod stays still until the two rods touch each other.
options.rationale: Expects nothing to happen across a gap, because a force is thought to require contact.

mcqs.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when they are not in contact?

options.text: A charged rod picks up small pieces of paper when it touches them.
options.rationale: Chosen because the effect is dramatic, but contact is part of the description, so it does not show a force acting across a gap.

options.text: A rubbed plastic rod picks up small iron filings from a nearby dish.
options.rationale: Attractive to students who think rubbing magnetises the rod; it also describes an effect that does not actually happen with iron filings.

options.text: A rubbed rod feels warmer than it did before it was rubbed.
options.rationale: True, and caused by friction, but it is evidence about heating rather than about any force between two objects.

options.text: A hanging charged rod turns away as a like charge is put near.
options.rationale: The rod starts to move while a visible gap remains, so the force must be acting across that gap. It is also repulsion, which rules out an uncharged object being attracted.

mcqs.stem: A charged polythene rod repels a second charged polythene rod. A student says this shows that rubbing has magnetised the rods. Why is the student wrong?

options.text: The force is electrostatic; rubbing only moves electrons.
options.rationale: Rubbing transfers charge, it does not magnetise. Polythene is not a magnetic material, and the rods behave differently from magnets.

options.text: Magnets repel across a gap, so the two effects must be the same.
options.rationale: Agrees with the student rather than correcting him, which appeals because both forces really do act at a distance.

options.text: Magnetism can only act when two poles are brought into contact.
options.rationale: Invents a contact rule for magnetism, which conflicts with the student's own experience of magnets repelling across a gap.

options.text: Two magnetised rods would always attract one another instead.
options.rationale: Half remembered: two magnets can attract or repel depending on which poles face, so this is not a reason to reject magnetism.

mcqs.stem: A student walks across a nylon carpet and then feels a small shock as her hand nears a metal door handle. What has happened?

options.text: The carpet made new charge, which was stored in the metal handle.
options.rationale: Charge is imagined as being created by the walking and as belonging to the handle, rather than transferred to the student.

options.text: Charge jumps from her hand only once her skin has touched it.
options.rationale: Denies that charge can cross air, even though the shock is felt as the hand approaches the handle.

options.text: Friction charged her up, and charge then crossed the air as a spark.
options.rationale: Rubbing between shoes and carpet transfers electrons, charging the student. The charge then crosses the gap to the earthed handle as a spark.

options.text: The flash is caused by heat from the friction of her shoes.
options.rationale: Explains the spark as a heating effect, because air is remembered as something that can never conduct.

mcqs.stem: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps across a gap to a nearby earthed metal pipe. Why does the spark happen?

options.text: Air can never conduct, so the light must come from the metal pipe.
options.rationale: Keeps the rule that air is always an insulator and looks for the flash somewhere else.

options.text: Charge can only cross a gap at the moment two surfaces touch.
options.rationale: Treats the air gap as a complete barrier, so the spark has to be relabelled as contact.

options.text: The charge on the object grows heavy enough to fall across.
options.rationale: Treats charge as a substance with weight that piles up and spills over, a picture built from the phrase charge builds up.

options.text: The field grows strong enough for the air in the gap to conduct.
options.rationale: As charge builds up, the electric field across the gap grows. Once it is strong enough the air stops insulating and charge flows across, which is the spark.

mcqs.stem: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth and both become positively charged. In terms of electrons, why do the rods then repel each other?

options.text: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the like charges repel.
options.rationale: Losing electrons leaves each rod positively charged, and two objects carrying the same type of charge push each other apart.

options.text: Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so both are now positive.
options.rationale: Gets the charge right but moves protons to explain it, which the question's wording about electrons should have blocked.

options.text: Rubbing made positive charge on each rod, which pushes them apart.
options.rationale: Answers without any electron transfer at all, treating the positive charge as something the rubbing manufactured.

options.text: Each rod lost an equal amount of charge, so the forces balance.
options.rationale: Confuses equal charges with balanced forces, and predicts no movement rather than repulsion.

options.text: A set of paths that a charged object has to follow.
options.rationale: Reads the drawn lines as tracks, helped by circuit diagrams where lines really do carry charge.

options.text: A region in which a charge experiences a force.
options.rationale: A charged object creates a field around itself, and a second charged object placed anywhere in that region feels a force.

options.text: Only the lines drawn around a charge on a diagram.
options.rationale: Confuses the model with the thing modelled, so the field exists only where a line has been drawn.

options.text: The charge that has built up on a rubbed object's surface.
options.rationale: Confuses the field with its source, a common slip when both are described using the same word, charge.

mcqs.stem: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change as you move further away from the sphere?

options.text: It gets stronger, because the field spreads out as it goes out.
options.rationale: Reads the widening fan of field lines as the field growing rather than thinning.

options.text: It stays the same up to the last line and then stops there.
options.rationale: Takes the edge of the drawing as the edge of the field, so the field is uniform and then absent.

options.text: It stays exactly the same all around the charged sphere.
options.rationale: Confuses the symmetry of the pattern, which is the same in every direction, with the strength, which changes with distance.

options.text: It gets weaker; the field is strongest close to the charged sphere.
options.rationale: The specification states it directly: the field is strongest close to the object and the further away you go, the weaker it is.

mcqs.stem: A charged object is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force between them?

options.text: The force gets stronger as the distance between them decreases.
options.rationale: The second object sits in a field that is stronger closer in, so the force on it increases as the gap closes.

options.text: The force stays the same, as it depends only on the two charges.
options.rationale: Charge is the quantity the student has been given, so it becomes the only thing the force is thought to depend on.

options.text: The force gets weaker, because the two fields start to cancel.
options.rationale: Borrows the idea of cancelling from wave superposition and applies it to two fields that are simply both present.

options.text: There is no force at all until the two objects touch.
options.rationale: Denies the non-contact force outright, which is the default expectation from everyday pushes and pulls.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated charged sphere?

options.text: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, all evenly spaced out.
options.rationale: Confuses the electric field pattern with the loops of a magnetic field or with contour lines on a map.

options.text: Straight lines spreading out from the sphere in all directions.
options.rationale: The pattern is radial: straight lines evenly spaced all around the sphere, closer together near the surface, with arrows away from a positive sphere.

options.text: Straight lines that always point inwards, towards the sphere itself.
options.rationale: Generalises from gravitational fields, which always point inwards, so a field is remembered as something that pulls.

options.text: Lines that get closer together further out from the sphere.
options.rationale: Remembers that the spacing carries meaning but reverses it, so the field would be strongest a long way from the sphere.

mcqs.stem: How does the idea of an electric field help to explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?

options.text: Each object sends out lines that pull the other one along them.
options.rationale: Treats the field lines as physical connectors, which makes the force a contact force again in disguise.

options.text: The objects interact only if a field line joins one to the other.
options.rationale: Restricts the field to the drawn lines, so the interaction depends on how the diagram happens to be drawn.

options.text: Each object sits in the other's field, so each feels a force.
options.rationale: The field fills the space around each charged object, so neither one has to reach the other: each is already inside a region where it experiences a force.

options.text: The air between the objects passes the push from one to the other.
options.rationale: Looks for a material to carry the force, because a force through empty space still feels as though it needs a medium.
